findings.source_grounded_note: Courtly imitation and French as an elite European language made events and literature in France unusually accessible abroad; a nascent nationalist backlash did not yet displace this dominance.

Semi-official papers, independent journals, clandestine Jansenist news, foreign French-language presses, and local/daily papers form distinct communication channels. Gazette de Leyde’s informed oppositional tilt differs from conservative and radical competitors.
Imprisonment interrupts neither Linguet’s journal nor his influence; prison memoirs sell an image of arbitrary incarceration and prompt publication outside royal jurisdiction.

Privilege, tacit permission, simple tolerance, independent Sorbonne/parlement action, contraband imports, tariffs, and Paris inspection differ in legal effect. Condemnation can advertise a book; regulation can raise general transport costs.

Literacy alone does not imply affordability. Cheap blue-library literature, subscription libraries, reading rooms, literary societies, and exclusive academies offer different access. Nobles, clergy, and professional bourgeois dominate cultivated reading more than merchants.

Loss of Jesuit colleges fragments curricula without national replacement. Classical/Catholic humanities coexist with increasingly experimental, Newtonian scientific instruction, supplying habits that might be applied to human institutions.

findings.topic: Enlightenment as rational criticism and popularization
findings.source_grounded_note: Philosophes seek practical improvement and happiness through criticism addressed to educated opinion. Voltaire’s English encounter introduces toleration, Locke, Newton, and Bacon; his later campaigning and celebrity provide a model for writers.

findings.topic: Montesquieu’s analysis, intermediary powers, and liberty
findings.source_grounded_note: Historical/natural circumstances limit institutional transfer; nobility and parlements check monarchical despotism. Separation/balance of powers is influential even though the English constitution is partly misunderstood. Preserve analysis versus prescription.

Diderot and d’Alembert transform a reference project into critical inquiry. Suspensions, Malesherbes’s tacit support, expanded editions, notoriety, and independent thought matter separately; later Diderot’s radicalism is not simply identical with the early project.

Rousseau’s claim that institutions corrupt natural goodness challenges Enlightenment confidence in material progress. Literary emotion and individual virtue differ from a programme for wholesale social change.

findings.topic: Social Contract, general will, and retrospective appropriation
findings.source_grounded_note: The text presents a theoretical legitimacy model for small states, not a direct political programme. General will is explicitly not necessarily majority will; later readers turn its formulas into a pattern for national regeneration.
Civil religion and the Savoyard curate’s natural religion trigger censure; condemnation should not be assigned simply to revolutionary political content.

Doctrinal/authority disputes, sacraments, convulsionaries, and Jansenist parliamentary action damage Church prestige. Philosophes’ claimed victory over Jesuits differs from the agency described by the author.

Less demonstrative devotion need not mean simple unbelief. Practical toleration grows before legal emancipation; Calas/Sirven campaigns and a Protestant minister expose the gap between penal law and conduct.

findings.topic: Criminal justice reform and public campaigning
findings.source_grounded_note: Calas, Damiens, and La Barre reveal different uses of exemplary punishment. Beccaria, torture reform, and uncensored legal briefs sustain a campaign against cruelty and miscarriages of justice.

findings.topic: Public opinion as tribunal and political force
findings.source_grounded_note: Opinion acquires the claim of informed authoritative judgment. Religious combatants and parlements precede philosophes; governments themselves defend policy in print, widening examination of the constitution.

findings.topic: Physiocracy’s natural order and powerful reforming state
findings.source_grounded_note: Quesnay’s agrarian productivity, Tableau économique, Mirabeau, Dupont, and Le Mercier offer economic freedom through removal of obstacles. Legal despotism is an apparent paradox: strong authority is needed to create free conditions and enlarge taxable wealth.

findings.topic: Seven Years War and discredited government
findings.source_grounded_note: Military failure, Austrian alliance, taxation, and borrowing provoke institutional scrutiny. Later royal marriage disaster, Du Barry, Terray’s bankruptcy, and Maupeou deepen distrust through different mechanisms.

findings.topic: Grain liberalization, scarcity, and paternal duty
findings.source_grounded_note: 1763–64 freedom collides with failing harvests; long-run production arguments conflict with immediate subsistence and the king’s protective duty. Reimposed contracting produces famine-pact suspicion rather than confidence.

Voltaire welcomes a strong reforming monarch; Diderot fears despotism without intermediaries. Parliamentary destruction generates renewed interest in the little-understood Estates-General; restoration fails to repair trust.

findings.topic: Royal reputation and Diamond Necklace Affair
findings.source_grounded_note: Rumour about sexual/marital failure and court conduct precedes the necklace fraud. The queen was uninvolved; Rohan’s acquittal, acclaim, and exile still disgrace the court. Preserve innocence versus public suspicion.

Activist administration attracts popular opposition and jurisdictional challenge even from elites who may share its ends. Provincial estates, landowner-assembly plans, and Necker’s Berry/upper Guyenne experiments should remain distinguishable.

findings.topic: Necker’s public career and alternative ministry
findings.source_grounded_note: Banking wealth, Suzanne Necker’s salon, controlled-grain advocacy, fiscal/administrative reform, and published self-defence cultivate popularity. Opinion cannot secure his policy ambitions in 1781 but sustains a claim to future recall.

findings.topic: America, representation, and the possibility of a new beginning
findings.source_grounded_note: Vergennes’s strategic success has intellectual costs. Raynal/Diderot, translated American documents, Franklin’s image, soldiers’ return, and criticism of hereditary Cincinnati spread distinct routes to liberty and institutional reconstruction.

Scientific marvels, mesmerism, and lodges express appetite for change. Masonry combines status hierarchy and female exclusion with internal equality/elected merit, charity, and judicial activism; most lodges avoid politics, and conspiracy suspicions are not proof of general subversion.

uncertainties.note: Necker’s financial management is referred onward to pages 66–68; maintain linkage to the next chunk rather than assigning those details solely to this page.
